# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm, Comment)

The first half of this comment is valuable. Using the microdata, it confirms several weaknesses that the Halden working paper's own numbers suggested: manager-reported output runs above organisations' records, the hours denominator overstates the cut in time, and revenue was compared in nominal terms. It also uncovers something new and important about attrition.

The second half is much weaker. The headline conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty," goes well beyond the comment's own corrected estimate. It is also contradicted by the randomised evidence the authors themselves cite.

Most numbers check out. I recomputed every row of Table 2 (98.7/0.8, 95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859, 95.4/0.861), the hours ratios (34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861), and the real-revenue figure (1.014/1.041 → −2.6%). There is one internal inconsistency, in the hours decomposition (see §3).

## 1. The central conclusion is not supported, and the comment's own best evidence contradicts it

- **The comment's corrected estimate is still a gain.** After correcting output and hours, it finds +10.8% per actual hour. Section 6 then concedes that "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." That supports *uncertain*, not *entirely an artifact*. Shifting the burden of proof is a reason to withhold judgement. It does not license the opposite positive claim.
- **The comment uses the Varden trial selectively.** It calls the Varden counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature to date," but omits the case-processing stratum of the same trial. That stratum found output per actual hour up 12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). It was randomised (so no selection problem), used record-based output and timesheet hours (so neither of the measurement problems), and the effect was still present at nine months. In other words, it addresses every source of artifact the comment names except possibly novelty. The Varden counter stratum also found a per-hour *gain* (+6.7%), which the comment does not mention.
- **The best-supported conclusion is narrower.** Per-hour gains are much smaller than uncontrolled pilots report. Per-employee output falls in work that depends on presence. Whether per-hour gains last is still open.
- **The scope is too broad.** "The per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" generalises from one re-analysed pilot to the whole literature.

## 2. Attrition: an important finding, but its effect is not quantified

- **This is the comment's most significant new fact.** The working paper says the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show that seven withdrew *after the schedule began*, and that most cited workload. If correct, this is a material misstatement in the working paper. The Halden Institute should correct it.
- **The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't.** The abstract says "correcting the first three [problems]" gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is not adjusted for anywhere, and the 10.8% subset consists of survivors only.
- **Even with no outcome data on the withdrawals, the effect can be bounded.** For example: if the nine had averaged output of 85 or 90, what would the pooled estimate be? Lee bounds or worst-case bounds would turn "plausibly the least successful" into a number. Without this, the claim in the conclusion that attrition "removed the organisations least able to cope" is stated more strongly than §1 supports. §1 itself says "plausibly."
- **One reason is missing.** Six withdrawals cited workload and two cited scheduling. That is eight of nine, so one reason is unaccounted for.

## 3. Measurement corrections: largely sound, with two caveats

- **"Billable hours delivered" is not a neutral output measure.** For professional-services firms, billable hours fall mechanically when hours fall. Some of the 3.8-point gap between manager-reported and record-based output may therefore reflect the records measuring input rather than output, not managers rounding up. The comparison should be reported by type of record, or with billable-hours organisations excluded.
- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** On a 32-hour schedule:
  - logged pilot hours are 34.6, so time worked beyond the schedule is 2.6 hours a week;
  - day-off work accounts for 1.6 of those hours, leaving 1.0 hour across the four working days, about 0.25 hours a day;
  - the text says +0.7 hours a day, which is 2.8 hours a week. Together with day-off work that would give about 36.4 hours, not 34.6.

  If the 0.7 is measured against baseline days of 8.06 hours, the gap is larger still. One of these figures needs correcting.
- **The subset comparisons don't line up.** Table 2's rows use different, non-nested subsets (61, 23, 27, 17). The step from 23.4% to 10.8% mixes the effect of the corrections with differences between the subsets. Showing all four specifications on the same 17 organisations would isolate the corrections. The data note acknowledges the subsets are non-random, but the abstract and conclusion don't carry that caveat.

## 4. Revenue

The point is correct, and I'd flagged it in the working paper. However, CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, because output prices in professional services or software can move quite differently from consumer prices. "Approximately" is doing a lot of work here. Sector-specific producer price indices would be better. The comment also slightly overstates the working paper's claim, which was "no sign that output was sacrificed," not that revenue grew. Revenue also has no bearing on the per-hour estimate, so it shouldn't be counted among problems that "account for most of the reported gain."

## 5. Sectoral claims

The mechanical point is right: any output index above 80 shows up as a per-hour gain. But "a fall of 11.2%" in retail and hospitality rests on **three organisations**. That is a thin basis for the comment's argument, and especially so given how §7 treats a seven-office correlation.

## 6. The novelty argument is the weakest section

- **The extrapolation is arithmetically off and methodologically weak.** A linear decline from 0.61 at month three to 0.29 at month six reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." More importantly, two points can't distinguish a linear decline from a plateau.
- **Energy is not output.** The comment infers that a productivity effect is fading from a decline in self-reported energy.
- **The direct test is available but not run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. The microdata should show whether output per hour declined from month to month. That is the test of novelty, and it is the most important analysis missing from the comment.
- **Varden's nine-month result counts against simple novelty.** The case-processing gain was still present after the point where the comment's own extrapolation reaches zero. This isn't conclusive, but it should be addressed.

## 7. The meetings section mischaracterises the Varden analysis and applies a double standard

- **The description is inaccurate.** The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known." They are all of the treated case-processing offices. The meeting data were collected at managers' request in month six. The Varden authors flagged the analysis as unregistered, warned that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test. The comment acknowledges none of this.
- **The scepticism is reasonable in substance.** In my earlier review I noted r = 0.71 with n = 7 gives p ≈ 0.07. But the comment applies a far stricter standard here than it does to its own three-organisation retail figure or its two-point extrapolation of energy.
- **The meetings hypothesis competes with novelty.** It offers an alternative to novelty as an explanation for any per-hour gain. Dismissing it removes a rival to the comment's preferred account. This deserves even-handed treatment, not a dismissal in one paragraph.

## 8. Smaller points

- In the conclusion, "attrition removed…" and "the output measure overstated output by roughly four points" are both stated more confidently than the evidence in §1 and §2. The four points also comes from a non-random subset of 23 organisations.
- The data note is good. Its caveats belong in the abstract too.
- The recommendations (record-based output, actual hours, comparison group, longer follow-up, intention-to-treat including withdrawals) are sound, and largely match Varden's design.

---

**Overall:** §§1–4 make a real contribution and should be published, with the hours decomposition fixed, the attrition effect bounded, and the corrections run on a common subset. §§6–8 and the conclusion should be rewritten. A conclusion the evidence supports would be roughly this: the Halden pilot's headline overstates the per-hour gain by at least half. A gain of about 11% remains in a subset of surviving organisations that is not representative. Randomised evidence shows a similar per-hour gain in backlog work and a per-employee loss in coverage-bound work. Whether these gains last is unresolved.

If you're writing a reply or a referee report on any of these three documents, I can draft it.
